findings.failure_mode: if any prior holder panics while holding the lock, the mutex becomes poisoned and every future call to process() will panic with a String payload, crashing the entire task
findings.fix: use match or ? to propagate PoisonError; return a typed error from process() and never unwrap a Mutex::lock() result

findings.problem: async fn process contains a 10M-iteration CPU-bound loop on the async executor
findings.failure_mode: std::sync::Mutex lock + 10M pushes blocks the tokio worker thread, starving all other async tasks on that executor; concurrent callers will see cascading latency
findings.fix: move the CPU work to a bounded Rayon pool or spawn_blocking; keep the async fn as an I/O coordination shell

findings.problem: std::sync::MutexGuard is held across the .await on line 9
findings.failure_mode: tokio holds the OS thread while the MutexGuard keeps the std::sync::Mutex locked during sleep(); the thread cannot drive other tasks, effectively serializing the entire async runtime on this lock
findings.fix: drop the guard before .await; restructure so the async boundary is inside the critical section or use a tokio::sync::Mutex if cross-task sharing is required

findings.problem: Arc<std::sync::Mutex<Vec<u64>>> is the wrong synchronization primitive for async code
findings.failure_mode: std::sync::Mutex blocks the underlying OS thread; in an async runtime this is equivalent to blocking the event loop thread. tokio::sync::Mutex or a message-passing design is required
findings.fix: replace std::sync::Mutex with tokio::sync::Mutex, or redesign with owned data per task and message passing (mpsc channel) to eliminate shared mutable state

findings.problem: 10M pushes into an unreserved Vec will trigger ~24 reallocations (geometric growth from default 4-capacity Vec)
findings.failure_mode: each reallocation copies all prior elements, causing O(n) amortized work per push but O(n^2) total memory bandwidth; OOM can occur during any grow; tail latency is dominated by allocator contention
findings.fix: pre-allocate with Vec::with_capacity(10_000_000) or accept a pre-sized buffer from the caller

findings.problem: Function signature returns () while performing fallible operations (Mutex lock, Vec push can OOM)
findings.failure_mode: allocation failure (Vec::push) returns Err(AllocError) at runtime which will panic; the API surface gives no way for callers to handle or distinguish lock failure from allocation failure
findings.fix: return Result<(), ProcessError> with a custom error enum covering LockError and ResourceError; use ? on lock() and push()

findings.problem: sleep(Duration::from_millis(1)).await after 10M iterations serves no apparent purpose and extends lock hold time
findings.failure_mode: the sleep() adds 1ms of latency while the std::sync::Mutex is still held, unnecessarily blocking the async executor thread and amplifying contention for any other holder of the shared Arc
findings.fix: remove the sleep() unless it models a specific I/O or backpressure requirement; if required, it must be documented and the mutex must be dropped before the await

findings.problem: The Vec is heap-allocated via Arc and grows dynamically with 10M u64 elements (~80MB)
findings.failure_mode: each call to process() appends 10M+ elements to the same shared Vec with no cap, unbounded growth, or capacity reset; memory usage grows without bound across invocations
findings.fix: declare a maximum capacity; reset or replace the Vec per invocation; or use a bounded ring buffer / circular buffer with a fixed maximum size

residual_risk: static review only; no commands run. The code has 4 BLOCKER violations (unwrap panic, CPU-bound async blocking, lock held across await, wrong mutex type), 4 MAJOR violations (unbounded reallocation, ignored fallible returns, unnecessary sleep extending lock hold, unbounded heap growth), and 7 missing evidence gaps (benchmarks, profiler, toolchain, second-ring evidence, allocation budget, contention measurement, release profile). The design is fundamentally incompatible with async Rust: a std::sync::Mutex protects a dynamically growing heap buffer while a 10M-iteration CPU loop runs on the async executor, with the lock held across an await point. Every blocking call in the async path will starve the executor.
